books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, July 1845

stimulus.source_note: John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, July 1845. Public domain.
stimulus.text: Texas is now ours. Already, before these words are written, her Convention has undoubtedly ratified the acceptance, by her of our proffered invitation into the Union... And that claim is by the right of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions. California will, probably, next fall away from the loose adhesion which, in such a country as Mexico, holds a remote province in a slight equivocal kind of dependence on the metropolis.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from John L. O'Sullivan, “Annexation,” July 1845, public domain
stem: The passage best illustrates which of the following developments in the 1840s?

options.text: The rise of organized opposition to slavery in the northern states.
options.misconception: O'Sullivan writes about expansion and annexation, not about the movement against slavery.

options.text: The federal government's purchase of Alaska from Russia.
options.misconception: Alaska was purchased in 1867, more than twenty years after this editorial.

options.text: The belief that the United States was destined to expand westward.
The growth of factory labor in the cities of the Northeast.
options.misconception: The passage is about land, Texas, and California, not about factories or city workers.

rationales.A: The passage argues for expansion, not for ending slavery; organized antislavery politics is a different development.
rationales.B: Alaska was bought from Russia in 1867, long after 1845, so it cannot be what an 1845 editorial illustrates.
rationales.C: O'Sullivan names the idea itself — “our manifest destiny to overspread the continent” — and applies it to Texas and then to California.
rationales.D: Nothing in the passage concerns factories or wage labor; it is about claiming land across the continent.
rationales.general:
1. Name what O'Sullivan is doing. He is arguing that Texas belongs in the Union and that California will follow.
2. Find the idea behind the argument. He calls it “our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence.”
3. Match that idea to the choices. Only one choice names a belief about spreading across the continent.
Remember: an editorial that coins a phrase is often the best evidence that the phrase's idea was alive in its moment.
